title: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies (c. 600 BCE-600 CE)

topics.title: Prinsep and Piyadassi: inscriptions as sources

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how James Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi and Kharosthi in the 1830s changed the study of early Indian political history.
Explain what inscriptions are, the languages they used and how undated inscriptions are dated.

topics.title: The earliest states: mahajanapadas and Magadha

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the main features of the sixteen mahajanapadas, including monarchies, ganas or sanghas and fortified capitals.
Compare the explanations of modern historians and early Buddhist and Jaina writers for the rise of Magadha.
Identify the sources used to reconstruct Mauryan history and what Asoka meant by dhamma.
Explain how the Mauryan Empire was administered through political centres, routes, the army and dhamma mahamattas.
Evaluate how important the Mauryan Empire was and why historians in colonial India valued it.
Distinguish chiefs from kings and describe the chiefdoms of the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas in Tamilakam.
Explain how the Kushanas used titles, statues and coins to project divine kingship.
Explain the role of samantas and assess prashastis such as the Prayaga Prashasti as historical sources.

topics.title: A changing countryside: subjects and agricultural production

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how historians use stories such as the Jatakas to understand what subjects thought of their rulers.
Describe plough agriculture, transplantation and irrigation as strategies for raising production, and their limits.

topics.title: Differences in rural society and land grants

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the categories of rural people named in Pali and Sangam texts, including the gahapati.
Analyse land grants, agraharas and the historians' debate on their impact.
Describe the location of early historic towns and the evidence of their elites, craftspersons and guilds.
Explain the land, river and sea routes of trade within the subcontinent and beyond.
Analyse what punch-marked, Indo-Greek, Kushana, Yaudheya and Gupta coins reveal about exchange.
Explain how Brahmi and Kharosthi were deciphered and how epigraphists identify the issuer of an inscription.
Evaluate the technical and fundamental limitations of inscriptional evidence.
